title: Zuma Game
summary: You play a Zuma game variation with a row of colored balls on a board and a set of balls in your hand.
statement: You play a Zuma game variation with a row of colored balls on a board and a set of balls in your hand. Each ball can be red 'R', yellow 'Y', blue 'B', green 'G', or white 'W'. Your objective is to clear the board by inserting balls from your hand. On each turn, pick a ball from your hand and place it between two balls on the board or at an end. If three or more consecutive balls of the same color form, remove them. Continue removing groups until no more groups can be removed. If the board is cleared, you win. If you run out of balls in your hand without clearing the board, you lose. Given the board's string and your hand's string, determine the minimum number of balls you must insert to clear the board. If it's impossible, return -1.
constraints: 1 <= len(board) <= 16 and 1 <= len(hand) <= 5. Every character is one of R, Y, B, G, W.
The initial board has no run of three or more equal colors. A move spends one ball from hand and inserts it into ANY gap, including either end.
After each insertion, remove a run of THREE OR MORE matching balls; continue all resulting chain reactions until the board is stable.
Return the minimum number of inserted balls that clears the whole board, or -1 if impossible. Unused hand balls are allowed.
An insertion that removes nothing immediately is legal and may be necessary. The remaining count of every hand color matters.
hints: A search state needs both the stable board and the remaining multiset of hand balls.
Combine exact insertion search with an optimistic interval-clearing bound. Try every available color in every distinct gap and fully resolve reactions; do not require immediate removal.
For each legal insertion, spend that color, collapse around the inserted position until stable, and minimize 1+search(next_board,remaining_hand). Empty board costs zero.

For a relaxed interval with k held matching balls, either pay max(0,2-k) to remove its first ball or clear an interior and join a later match. Cap k at two. This ignores inventory and forced reactions, so its cost is a lower bound: if it exceeds the hand size, stop. Identical insertion positions and mirrored boards can also be merged safely.
editorial: The hand contains at most five balls, so enumerate bounded insertion sequences with memoization on (stable board, sorted remaining hand). Full chain reactions are resolved around the insertion seam. Deleting a group can create another matching group on that seam, including a group of four or more. Only exact duplicate positions and mirror-symmetric boards are merged. For every color still on the board, at least max(0,3-board_count) balls of that color must be available; summing these deficits gives an admissible move lower bound. A nonempty stable board needs at least one move. Reaching that bound permits an early return, but no non-removing move type is discarded. An interval DP supplies another lower bound: allow unlimited inserted colors and allow matching balls to be held apart until their interior disappears. cost(l,r,k) either completes the first ball plus k held copies, or clears an interior interval and joins a later matching original ball. Held counts saturate at two. This relaxed game includes every real deletion sequence and can only require fewer insertions; a bound above the remaining hand size proves impossibility. Do not compress original matching runs in this DP, since a preparatory insertion may split one. For RRWWRRBBRR with hand WB, insert B between the first two R balls, then insert W into WW: the W, R, B, and R groups disappear in successive reactions. Completing an existing group first misses this two-move solution. The independent oracle uses breadth-first search over every hand index and every gap, with global run rescanning and no feasibility or symmetry pruning. Two adversarial full-size impossible boards also have independent bounded shortest-path certificates in a relaxed partial-run deletion game. Here n=len(board), h=len(hand), and S is the number of memoized states; the search remains exponential in h, bounded by the source limit h<=5.

tests.explanation: There are only two white balls in total and no white ball in hand, so no group can ever remove the whites. Clearing the red and blue groups still leaves WW; return -1.
Insert R into RR, leaving WWBBWW. Insert B into BB: removing BBB joins four white balls, which also disappear. Two insertions suffice, and each of the red/blue pairs needs at least one.
